entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Publius Attius Varus, a staunch adherent of Pompey the Great, was a Roman governor and military commander whose career became inextricably linked with the brutal struggle of Caesar's Civil War (49–45 BCE). His resistance in North Africa presented a significant early challenge to Julius Caesar's ambitions for control of the Roman Republic, placing him at the heart of pivotal campaigns that determined the fate of the Mediterranean world. As a former propraetor of Africa, Varus leveraged his local connections and military experience to rally forces against the Caesarian faction, embodying the deep political schism that tore the Republic apart.

Following the outbreak of civil war in 49 BCE, Varus was dispatched to take command of the province of Africa, quickly recruiting two legions to defend Pompey's interests. He initially achieved a notable victory against Gaius Scribonius Curio, Caesar's legate, at the Battle of Utica in 49 BCE, where Curio's forces were routed and Curio himself perished. This early success solidified Pompeian control over Africa and provided a crucial base of operations for the anti-Caesarian forces. Varus subsequently allied with King Juba I of Numidia and other Pompeian commanders like Quintus Caecilius Metellus Pius Scipio Nasica, participating in the protracted African campaign that culminated in the Battle of Thapsus in 46 BCE.
